stories.exam_facts: The columnist argues that without a reliable bond market, banks take on dangerous timing mismatches between short-term deposits and long-term loans; without active currency forward markets, businesses raise their prices to protect themselves against sudden exchange-rate swings; and without deep stock markets, institutional investors stay away and poor corporate management goes unpunished. The columnist argues that commercial banks buy the vast majority of new corporate bonds and sukuk issues and lock them away until maturity, so a bond that never trades in the secondary market is simply a bank loan in disguise, and that even in government securities, where trading on Bangladesh Bank's electronic platform has grown, the market still lacks a continuous, reliable benchmark for long-term interest rates. In the columnist's example, a manufacturer wanting to build a factory that takes seven to ten years to pay off cannot easily raise money through a ten-year fixed-rate bond, because large non-bank institutions such as insurance companies and pension funds refuse to buy long-term bonds they cannot easily sell; the manufacturer must instead rely on bank financing whose interest rates change every six to twelve months, while around 70 per cent of bank deposits mature within a single year.
